hook.text: Two lines of identical length. Add inward arrows to one and outward arrows to the other. Now one looks longer.

buildup.text: The Müller-Lyer illusion has fooled people since 1889. Even knowing it's an illusion doesn't make it disappear.

discovery.text: One theory: the arrows mimic depth cues from corners. Inward arrows look like an inside corner (closer, so seems bigger).

twist.text: But people from cultures without rectangular buildings—like the San people—are barely affected by the illusion.

climax.text: This illusion isn't hardwired. It's learned from a lifetime of processing a carpentered, right-angled environment.

punchline.text: Your illusions are shaped by the world you grew up in.

quiz.question: Why are some cultures less affected by the Müller-Lyer illusion?
options: Their environment has fewer right angles
They are trained to resist it
